caption: Specification-driven execution connects generation, auditing, and delivery through guarded tool use.
problem: Make recurring enterprise engineering tasks more consistent while measuring the value of AI assistance.
contribution: Built workflows for generation, auditing, and validation; implemented specification-driven execution with pre- and post-tool guardrails.
decision: Tool execution has checks before and after a call. This creates explicit places to constrain actions and inspect generated changes alongside the delivery pipeline.
evidence: Reported outcomes: 1,875+ engineering hours saved across 238 tasks; 90.8% backend and 88.6% frontend accuracy.
limit: The current case study does not specify the time-saving baseline or accuracy rubric. These figures describe the reported initiative outcomes.

caption: The orchestrator coordinates 13 agent roles across 22+ repositories. KB-assisted reproduction identifies the affected service, categorization selects the frontend/backend paths, and PR-impact analysis gates implementation. Developer review controls merge and feeds reiteration and retrospective learning.
problem: Resolve frontend-reported bugs across a microservice architecture spanning more than 22 repositories. More than 90% of issues arrive through the frontend, even when the underlying fault belongs to a backend service.
contribution: Implemented an orchestrated bug-resolution workflow with Jira analysis, KB-assisted repo detection, bug categorization, frontend and backend investigation, fix proposals, PR-impact analysis, implementation, validation, and developer-driven reiteration.
decision: Reproduce the frontend symptom before choosing a repository. Use exact microservice-to-API mappings from the KB to find the responsible service. Categorize the fault as frontend-only, backend-only, or both, and invoke the applicable agents. Generate a proposal first, check open PRs for impact, and implement only after the green signal.
evidence: Reported evaluation: 84% success across 42 defects and 207+ engineering hours saved.
limit: The agent validates changes and raises a PR; the developer pulls the bug branch, verifies the fix, and controls merge. Unresolved issues return with developer feedback. After reiteration, the retrospective logs first-iteration mistakes to guide improvement. The frontend quickfix invocation trigger and blocked PR-impact handling are not yet specified.
next: Add an anonymized bug trace showing the reproduction, KB-based service mapping, selected route, impact-scan result, validation, and any developer-feedback iteration.
steps: The orchestrator coordinates the specialist agents and owns the final PR handoff. The system works across a microservice architecture with more than 22 repositories.
The Jira analysis agent fetches and analyzes the issue. More than 90% of bugs are reported through the frontend, so the workflow starts with the user-visible symptom.

The repo detection agent reproduces the bug from the frontend and consults the knowledge base to locate the affected microservice and repository. If the API is not failing, it identifies the frontend as the issue or at least the relevant repository.
The knowledge base maps each microservice to its APIs. It supplies routing context to repo detection; it is a supporting knowledge source, not a sub-agent.
The bug categorization agent determines whether the issue is frontend-only, backend-only, or spans both. Only the relevant investigation and fix paths are invoked.
The frontend investigation agent investigates the UI-side behavior when the issue is frontend-only or affects both layers.
The backend infra investigation agent investigates the backend side when the issue is backend-only or spans both layers.

The frontend fix execution agent first generates a fix proposal. After a green signal from PR-impact analysis, it updates the proposed fix if needed or implements the code. It does not bypass the impact gate.
The backend fix execution agent first generates a fix proposal. After PR-impact analysis gives a green signal, it updates the fix if needed or implements the code.
The PR-impact scan agent checks whether any open PR could affect the proposed fix. Fix execution proceeds only after a green signal. The exact handling of a blocked scan is not specified here.
The frontend validation agent validates the frontend implementation before the orchestrator raises the PR.
The backend validation agent validates the backend implementation before the orchestrator raises the PR.

The frontend quickfix agent is part of the agent roster. Its invocation trigger and position in the workflow have not yet been specified, so it is shown as an available specialist without a presumed execution path.
After the applicable validation agents validate the fix, the orchestrator raises the pull request for developer review.
The developer pulls the bug branch and validates the fix. If it resolves the issue, the developer merges it. Otherwise, additional developer input is returned to the agent for another iteration.

When developer validation finds the issue unresolved, the agent reiterates the bug with the additional developer inputs, revisiting the relevant investigation, proposal, PR-impact, implementation, and validation stages.
After reiteration, the self-healing retrospective agent logs mistakes from the first iteration and uses those recorded lessons to help improve future agent behavior.
Merge happens after developer validation confirms that the bug is fixed. The agent raises the PR; developer approval controls the merge.
summary: An orchestrator coordinates 13 agent roles to resolve Jira bugs across 22+ repositories. Frontend reproduction and a microservice/API knowledge base identify the affected service, followed by targeted investigation, gated fixes, validation, and developer review.
subtitle: From frontend symptom to the right microservice, validated fix, and developer-reviewed PR.

caption: Admin documents are parsed by heading, with image descriptions, alt text, and source references incorporated before embedding. Learner state and skills context support JEV-based query refinement; RAG supplies relevant material for a prompt package. The LLM selects and populates a predefined template, and course completion updates learner state.
problem: Create small personalized courses from source documents while accounting for a learner's metadata, existing skills, and evolving learning state.
contribution: Built the learning pipeline spanning admin document ingestion, heading-based chunking, vision-based image descriptions, embeddings and metadata storage, JEV-based query refinement, RAG, prompt packaging, and template-based course assembly.
decision: Use three distinct data stores: learner current state, vector database, and skills graph. Replace extracted images with vision-generated descriptions plus alt text and reference location before embedding. Refine queries using JEV and learner context before retrieval. Give the LLM predefined frontend templates to choose and populate.
evidence: The described implementation turns uploaded source documents into a small personalized course, then updates learner state after completion. The architecture includes both admin ingestion and the learner delivery loop.
limit: Course completion updates learner current state. The provided implementation details do not specify the skills-graph traversal, JEV internals, or measured course-quality results.
next: Add an anonymized example showing a document heading and image, the resulting enriched chunk, a learner's original and refined query, the chosen course template, and the learner-state update after completion.
title: Learnware AI
subtitle: From source documents to a personalized course, with a learner-state feedback loop.
summary: A personalized learning system with three data stores: learner current state, a vector database, and a skills graph. Heading-based document chunks and vision-generated image descriptions feed retrieval; JEV refines learner queries before an LLM assembles a course using predefined frontend templates.
steps: An admin uploads the source documents that supply the learning content.
The document parser extracts content and creates chunks based on document headings, retaining the section-based organization.

Vision models generate descriptions of images. Each description replaces the image in the extracted content, together with its alt text and reference location. This walkthrough illustrates a source document containing images.
The system generates embeddings for the prepared content, including the textual descriptions that stand in for images, and associates metadata with the chunks.
The vector database stores embeddings and their metadata. RAG later retrieves relevant source content from this indexed material.
The learner submits a learning request, such as: I want to learn AI.

The learner-current-state database stores the metadata and current skill set used for personalization. JEV uses this learner context when refining the query. After course completion, this same store is updated for future requests.

The skills graph is the third data store alongside learner current state and the vector database. It represents skills context in the learning architecture; the specific graph traversal logic has not been described.
The JEV decision model expands or refines the learning query based on learner metadata and the current skill set before retrieval.
RAG uses the refined query to extract relevant documents from the vector database.
The system creates a prompt package containing the information needed for an LLM to build a small personalized course, including the learning request, learner context, and retrieved content.
Predefined frontend templates provide the available presentation layouts. The LLM chooses an appropriate template and feeds course data into it.
The LLM uses the prompt package to assemble the personalized course by selecting an appropriate predefined template and populating it with data.
The completed course is presented to the learner using the selected frontend template.
After the learner completes the course, the system updates the learner-current-state database. The updated state informs personalization when the learner returns with another request.
impact: ⚡ 3 data stores · JEV-refined RAG · learner-state feedback

caption: Resume ingestion extracts text, parses structured profiles, and indexes three local MiniLM embeddings per resume. Screening parses a JD, blends full-profile and skills searches, loads profiles from PostgreSQL, applies six knockout rules, and scores eligible candidates. Explicit branches cover knockout failures and degraded search/scoring before persisted results reach the recruiter.
problem: Screen a pool of resumes against a structured job description while combining semantic relevance, explicit eligibility rules, and contextual scoring with recruiter-readable explanations.
contribution: Project scope covers a JWT-protected Next.js/FastAPI application, asynchronous PDF/DOCX ingestion, Gemini-based resume and JD parsing, local multi-view embeddings, Pinecone retrieval, deterministic knockout rules, scoring fallbacks, and persisted recruiter results.
decision: Separate resume ingestion from screening. Index three semantic views per resume, generate JD query vectors on demand, blend two semantic searches equally, and hydrate profiles from PostgreSQL. Apply hard eligibility rules before the more expensive Gemini scoring stage, then rank passed candidates by weighted fit score.
evidence: The supplied Technical Architecture & Flow Documentation (version 1.0, February 2026) describes the components, processing sequence, formulas, fallback behavior, async concurrency, progress polling, and CSV export. No measured ranking-accuracy or production-scale benchmark is provided.
limit: The document identifies shared Pinecone namespaces, post-retrieval filtering, ephemeral /tmp file storage, absent skill normalization/ontology and keyword-vector retrieval, and no recruiter-feedback learning loop. Redis is provisioned but not integrated. Tagging, namespace isolation, persistent object storage, and caching are proposed improvements, not completed capabilities.
next: Evaluate retrieval and ranking against a labeled candidate set, test each knockout and unavailable-service branch, and address durable file storage and tenant isolation before presenting the design as production-ready.
title: HireFlow
subtitle: Resume ingestion, dual-vector retrieval, deterministic rules, and explainable candidate ranking.
summary: A Next.js and FastAPI screening application that parses resumes and job descriptions with Gemini, indexes three 384-dimensional resume vectors in Pinecone, and combines semantic retrieval with six knockout rules and weighted candidate scoring. PostgreSQL stores profiles, jobs, progress, and results.
impact: ⚡ 3 resume vectors · 6 knockout rules · 4 scoring dimensions
steps: Recruiters use a Next.js 15 / React 19 interface to authenticate, upload resumes, create jobs, screen candidates, review results, shortlist, and export CSV. NextAuth manages the frontend session.

FastAPI validates JWT-protected requests and coordinates PostgreSQL, file handling, embeddings, Pinecone, and Gemini. Resume processing uses background tasks with up to five concurrent files per batch; candidate scoring uses up to three concurrent candidates. The frontend polls progress and can retrieve partial screening results.

The upload flow accepts PDF/DOCX files, with documented limits of 200 files per batch and 10 MB per file. Validation happens on both client and server. Files are saved under /tmp/hireflow_uploads/; this is local ephemeral storage, so persistence across container restarts is an identified gap.

PostgreSQL stores users, job_descriptions, upload_batches, resumes, and screening_results through async SQLAlchemy. Resume records hold file metadata, parsed candidate JSON, denormalized candidate fields, parse status, and Pinecone IDs. Job requirements and screening outcomes also persist here.
A background worker extracts all PDF pages using pdfplumber or DOCX paragraphs and tables using python-docx, producing one resume text string.

Gemini 2.0 Flash converts extracted resume text into structured candidate JSON: identity, skills, experience, education, certifications, and employment gaps. The documented parser retries up to three times with exponential backoff and uses safe defaults if parsing still fails.

Local sentence-transformers inference with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 generates three 384-dimensional vectors per resume: full profile, skills, and experience. These are specialized views of one resume; the current implementation does not perform text chunking.

Pinecone stores the three resume vectors with metadata, using cosine similarity. The default namespace is shared, and the document describes user_id filtering after retrieval; per-tenant namespace isolation and metadata pre-filtering remain gaps.
Gemini parses raw job-description text into structured requirements, including required skills, experience, education, and accepted locations. The parsed job is saved in PostgreSQL before screening.
At screening time, MiniLM generates two fresh 384-dimensional JD vectors: full job meaning and required skills. These serve as search queries and are not persistently indexed in Pinecone.

Two parallel semantic searches compare JD full against resume full-profile vectors and JD requirements against resume-skills vectors. Scores are combined 50%/50%. The candidate pool uses K = min(max_candidates x 3, 100), so 100 is a cap rather than a fixed count. This is dual-vector semantic search, not BM25 plus vector retrieval.
Retrieved resume IDs are hydrated from PostgreSQL to obtain the full parsed profiles required for knockout checks and candidate scoring.

Six deterministic rules check experience, mandatory skills, recent experience relevance, employment gaps, location/relocation, and education. Failure of any rule marks the candidate as knockout-failed. Only candidates passing all rules proceed to contextual scoring.

For candidates who pass the knockout gate, Gemini 2.0 Flash evaluates skills match, experience relevance, career progression, and measurable achievements. It also returns strengths, weaknesses, matched/missing skills, and a written match explanation.

The fit score combines skills 40%, experience 25%, career progression 20%, and measurable achievements 15%. Passing candidates are ordered by descending fit score and receive ranks. Score tiers are EXCELLENT (86-100), GOOD (61-85), ADEQUATE (31-60), and POOR (0-30).

Screening outcomes are persisted incrementally in PostgreSQL, including scores, tiers, ranks, explanations, and knockout failures. Passing candidates sort ahead of failed candidates. Errors for one candidate are isolated so remaining candidates can continue processing.

The frontend polls progress and fetches persisted candidate cards. Recruiters review the ranking, shortlist candidates, and export CSV. Failed-knockout candidates remain at the bottom with rank 0; shortlisting is stored but does not train a feedback model in the documented implementation.
A candidate failing any knockout rule bypasses AI scoring. Failure reasons are persisted, and the candidate is retained at the bottom of results with rank 0.

When Pinecone is unavailable, the documented degraded path queries PostgreSQL for recent resumes. It supplies a candidate pool without semantic relevance ranking, after which the normal eligibility and scoring pipeline can continue.

When Gemini scoring is unavailable, deterministic formulas derived from parsed resume fields supply the four category scores. Weighted aggregation still follows the same 40/25/20/15 fit-score formula. This fallback is separate from resume-parser retry/default handling.
scenario_note: Choose ingestion, screening, a failed knockout, or an unavailable-service path. These walkthroughs illustrate the documented implementation; they do not execute screening or evaluate real candidates.

study_sections.label: Two different weight systems
study_sections.text: Retrieval blends full-profile and skills cosine scores 50%/50% to select a capped candidate pool. Final fit scoring is a separate calculation: skills 40%, experience 25%, career progression 20%, achievements 15%.

study_sections.label: Six eligibility rules
study_sections.text: The documented rules check experience below 60% of the requirement; missing top-three mandatory recent skills; recent-skill overlap below 20%; an employment gap over 12 months; location mismatch without accepted relocation; and unmatched education-level keywords. These are implemented heuristics described by the document, not evidence of their effectiveness.

study_sections.label: Architecture source
study_sections.text: Based on the supplied HireFlow Technical Architecture & Flow Documentation, version 1.0, February 2026, especially sections 3-6 and 8-11. Recommendations in sections 12 and 14 are kept separate from current behavior.

caption: Registration stores one reference photo per student. Marking attendance converts that photo and every live face into 128-d dlib encodings, measures the Euclidean distance between them, and accepts a match at 0.6 or less. A match passes a once-per-day duplicate check before MySQL records it; a multi-face mode compares each live face against all enrolled encodings.
problem: Take class attendance from a webcam instead of a manual roll call, confirm that the person present is the registered student, and count each student once per subject per day.
contribution: Project scope covers webcam registration, face encoding and distance-based matching with the face_recognition library, per-subject daily attendance in MySQL with a duplicate check, a PyQt5 interface for registering, marking, and viewing attendance, and a multi-face mode that identifies everyone in view.
decision: Matching works on face encodings rather than raw pixels: each face is reduced to 128 numbers that stay similar for the same person across photos, so a comparison is a single distance calculation. The main app verifies the face against the student who entered the roll number (1:1), which needs one comparison and cannot confuse two enrolled students. The multi-face mode searches all enrolled encodings (1:N) to identify everyone in view without typed input.
evidence: The public source code shows the full registration, matching, and attendance flow. Reported result: 92% live recognition accuracy; the test conditions behind that figure are not yet documented.
limit: Each student is matched against a single reference photo, and the library's default 0.6 tolerance is used without tuning. Lighting, camera angle, and the number of enrolled students behind the 92% figure are not recorded, and false matches and missed matches are not reported separately.
next: Measure false-match and missed-match rates across lighting and camera angles, tune the tolerance from those results, enroll several photos per student, add a liveness check, and in multi-face mode select the closest match rather than the first within tolerance.
subtitle: Face encodings, distance-based matching, and per-subject attendance in a PyQt5 desktop app.
summary: A PyQt5 desktop app that registers students from a webcam photo and marks attendance by face. Each face becomes a 128-dimensional dlib encoding, and a live face matches when its Euclidean distance to the stored encoding is 0.6 or less. MySQL keeps students and one attendance table per subject and day; a multi-face mode identifies everyone in view against all enrolled encodings.
steps: The PyQt5 desktop window has four pages: Home, Register, Mark Attendance, and View Attendance. Each page collects a name, roll number, subject, or day and starts the matching flow.
MySQL holds a students table (name, roll number, class) and one attendance table per subject and day, each storing roll numbers with timestamps.
Each registered student has one reference photo, saved as dataset/{roll}.jpg. Every later comparison is made against these photos.
Registration opens an OpenCV webcam preview. Space captures the current frame as the student's reference photo; Esc cancels.

Before saving, the app confirms the roll number is not already in the students table. A new student gets a reference photo and a students row; a repeated roll number gets an "already registered" message.

To mark attendance, the student enters a roll number and subject. The app loads only that student's reference photo, detects the face, and converts it into a 128-number face encoding. The live face is then checked against this single encoding: 1:1 verification.

For recognizing anyone in view, embeddings.py encodes every reference photo up front. Photos with exactly one detected face are kept; their encodings are saved to embeddings.txt and the matching names to name.txt, forming a gallery of all enrolled faces for 1:N identification.
OpenCV reads webcam frames continuously. Each frame is processed on its own until a match is found or Esc is pressed.
The face_recognition library's default HOG (histogram of oriented gradients) detector scans the frame and returns a bounding box for every face, so several people can appear in one frame.

For each box, a facial-landmark model locates the eyes and nose to align the face, and dlib's ResNet network converts it into a 128-dimensional encoding. Photos of the same person produce encodings that sit close together; different people sit further apart.

Each live encoding is compared with the reference by Euclidean distance, the straight-line gap between two 128-number vectors. In 1:1 mode there is one reference encoding; in 1:N mode the live face is measured against every enrolled encoding.
compare_faces treats a distance of 0.6 or less as the same person, the library's default tolerance. A lower tolerance is stricter (fewer false matches, more misses); a higher one is more lenient.
If no face in the frame is within tolerance, nothing is recorded and the loop moves on to the next frame. Pressing Esc stops scanning.
In 1:1 mode a match confirms that the person at the camera is the student who entered the roll number. A green box and the roll number are drawn on the live frame.
In 1:N mode the first enrolled encoding within tolerance supplies the student's name from name.txt. The name is drawn on the frame and passed on for attendance logging.
The attendance table for the subject and day is created on first use. The app then checks whether the roll number already has an entry, so each student is counted once per subject per day.
If the roll number is already present, no new row is added and a popup reports that attendance was already marked.
In 1:N mode each recognized name is written once to Attendance.json with the time it was first seen.
A new entry stores the roll number and timestamp in MySQL, and a popup confirms that attendance was marked.
The View Attendance page takes a subject and day, reads that attendance table from MySQL, and lists roll numbers with their times.
scenario_note: Choose registration, a successful match, a repeat check-in, a frame with no match, multi-face identification, or viewing records. These walkthroughs illustrate the code path; they do not use a camera or recognize real faces.

study_sections.label: How two faces are compared
study_sections.text: Detect the face with HOG, align it using facial landmarks, encode it with dlib's ResNet into 128 numbers, then measure the Euclidean distance to the reference encoding. A distance of 0.6 or less counts as the same person. The network was trained so that photos of one person land close together, which lets a single threshold separate "same" from "different".

study_sections.label: 1:1 verification vs 1:N identification
study_sections.text: Verification answers "is this the student who entered this roll number?" with one comparison. Identification answers "who is this?" by comparing against every enrolled face, so its work and its chance of a false match grow with class size.

study_sections.label: Model benchmark vs this system
study_sections.text: The face_recognition library reports 99.38% accuracy for its dlib model on the Labeled Faces in the Wild benchmark. That describes the model on curated photos; the 92% figure is this project's live webcam result.

study_sections.label: Architecture source
study_sections.text: Based on the public repository mahesh1112/face_recognition, Attendance System folder: test.py (PyQt5 app), dataset.py (registration), test2.py (1:1 attendance marking), and embeddings.py with main.py (multi-face mode).
